title: Liveness, readiness and startup probes
summary: How Kubernetes knows a container is alive, ready, or still warming up.

steps.title: Three questions
body: | **readiness** | should this pod receive traffic *now*? | removed from Service endpoints (not restarted) |
| **liveness** | is the process stuck beyond repair? | container **restarted** |
| **startup** | has it finished starting? | liveness/readiness wait; restarted if it never starts |
failureThreshold: 30       # allows up to 150 s to start
Probes can be `httpGet` (2xx/3xx passes), `tcpSocket`, `grpc`, or `exec` (exit 0 passes). In ASP.NET Core, `app.MapHealthChecks("/health/ready")` with tagged checks gives you both endpoints.

steps.prompt: Match the situation to the probe that handles it.
pairs: app is warming a 2-minute cache at boot
database is briefly down; stop sending this pod requests but don't kill it
a deadlock: the process is alive but answers nothing, forever
the health check is "does `/tmp/healthy` exist?" rather than an HTTP call

steps.prompt: Your liveness probe calls `/health`, which checks the database. The database has a 30-second outage. What happens?
options: Every replica fails liveness and is restarted, turning a short DB blip into a full outage and restart storm
Pods are removed from the Service until the DB returns, then come back
steps.explain: Liveness should check only the process itself. Put dependency checks in **readiness**, and even there be careful: if all replicas go unready at once, the Service has no endpoints.

steps.prompt: Complete the probes: restart if `/live` fails 3 times, stop traffic if `/ready` fails.

steps.title: Probe timing
body: A probe runs every `periodSeconds`. After `failureThreshold` **consecutive** failures, it acts. One success resets the count (`successThreshold` is 1 for liveness).
t=0  ok   t=10 FAIL(1)  t=20 FAIL(2)  t=30 ok(reset)  t=40 FAIL(1) t=50 FAIL(2) t=60 FAIL(3) -> restart

Worst-case time to detect a hang ≈ `periodSeconds × failureThreshold` (+ `timeoutSeconds`). Set `initialDelaySeconds` or, better, a startup probe so slow starts are not mistaken for hangs: a liveness probe that fires during startup produces an endless restart loop that looks like `CrashLoopBackOff`.

steps.prompt: A pod's readiness probe never passes, but the process does not crash. What does `kubectl get pods` show in the READY and STATUS columns? Type them as `READY STATUS`.
steps.explain: Running but not Ready: the container is up, so no restart; it is just not an endpoint. `kubectl describe pod` shows *Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503*.

steps.prompt: A pod starts. Put the probe phases in the order they happen.
lines: Startup probe runs until it succeeds once
Readiness succeeds and the pod is added to Service endpoints
Later, liveness fails 3 times in a row and the container is restarted
steps.explain: While a startup probe is defined, liveness and readiness are held back. After a restart, the startup probe runs again.

steps.title: Stop a liveness probe from killing a healthy app
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `api` (traefik/whoami, which answers `GET /health` on port 80) keeps restarting:
`kubectl get pods` shows a growing RESTARTS count, and `kubectl describe pod -l app=api` tells you why.
Fix the Deployment so that the **liveness** probe checks `/health` on the app's real port, and add a **readiness**
probe on the same endpoint. The new pod must then stay up without restarts, and be Ready.

checks.name: api has stopped restarting and is Ready
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=40s >/dev/null && sleep 6 && kubectl get pods -l app=api -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null)] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .status.containerStatuses[0] | "\(.restartCount) \(.ready)"'
checks.fail: The new `api` pod still restarts, or is not Ready.

checks.name: the liveness probe checks /health on the app's port
checks.fail: Keep a liveness probe, aimed at whoami's `/health` on the container port (`80`, or its name `http`).

checks.name: a readiness probe gates traffic
checks.fail: Add a readiness probe on `/health` too.

hints: `kubectl describe pod -l app=api` shows `Liveness probe failed: ... connection refused` and `Killing`.
The probe asks `/healthz` on port 8080; whoami serves `/health` on port 80 (named `http`).
`kubectl patch deploy api --type=json` with `replace` on `/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/httpGet` and `add` of a `readinessProbe`.
solution: kubectl describe pod -l app=api | grep -E 'Liveness|Killing' | tail -n 3
steps.explain: A liveness probe that fails restarts the container, so a wrong path or port turns a healthy app into a restart loop, and a liveness probe that checks dependencies (the database) turns one outage into a cluster-wide restart storm. Readiness only removes the pod from Service endpoints. Keep liveness cheap and local, readiness honest, and use a `startupProbe` for slow starters.

steps.title: Build it: running, but not Ready
prompt: The pods say `Running` but `0/1 READY`. In the **Kubernetes builder**, look at where the readiness probe knocks and fix it (without removing the probe).
steps.explain: Traffic only goes to pods whose readiness probe passes. A probe on the wrong port keeps a healthy app out of service forever.
